# Sunakkhatta Sutta (MN 105 (PTS MN ii 252))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Sunakkhatta Sutta* (MN 105; PTS MN ii 252) is the 105th discourse of the Majjhimanikāya [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Set at the Peaked Roof Hall in the Great Wood outside Vesālī, the sutta is addressed to the Licchavi prince Sunakkhatta [McTighe; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The discourse was prompted by a number of monks declaring final knowledge (*aññā*) before the Buddha, leading to an exposition on how spiritual seekers may overestimate their meditative progress and declare awakening without having genuinely eradicated the fetters [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Rogell 2003]. The Buddha explains the nature of sensual attachment and genuine arahantship, insisting that true spiritual liberation requires an irreversible letting go of all causes of suffering [SuttaCentral; McTighe; Rogell 2003].
A prominent feature of the sutta is the medical allegory of the poisoned arrow (MN ii 259–260) [Shonin et al. 2015; Anālayo, From Craving to Liberation; eJournal of Buddhist Research Studies 2015]. In this extended simile, the wound represents the six internal sense bases, the arrow smeared with the poison of ignorance represents craving, the surgical probe represents mindfulness, the scalpel represents noble wisdom, and the skilled physician represents the Tathāgata who surgically extracts the shaft and expels the poison completely [Shonin et al. 2015; Humphreys 1956; Anālayo, From Craving to Liberation]. Lambert Schmithausen notes the sutta's distinctive metaphorical use of *sa-upādisesa* and *anupādisesa* with reference to residual infection or remaining traces of poison in a wound [Schmithausen 2014].
In Sanskrit Buddhist transmission, the text is identified under the title *Śalyasūtra* [Schmithausen 2014; Hartmann & Wille, Schøyen IV]. Extant witnesses include Sanskrit manuscript fragments cataloged as SHT sutta 35 and a folio fragment published from the Schøyen Collection [SuttaCentral; Hartmann & Wille, Schøyen IV]. DharmaNexus detects cross-language alignments with passages in the Sanskrit *Arthaviniścayasūtra* and *Saṅghabhedavastu*, Chinese translations in the *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) and *Ekottarikāgama* (T 125), and Tibetan canonical works [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also records extensive Pali-internal text reuse (2,555 matching passages across 144 texts), sharing major doctrinal passages with the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35), the *Aṭṭhakanipāta* (AN 8), the *Nidāna Saṁyutta* (SN 12), and other collections [DharmaNexus].
